newsitem.title: GERMANY: German grain lacks fizz as trade meets in Bremen.
newsitem.headline: German grain lacks fizz as trade meets in Bremen.

text.p: Northern German grain market activity will remain thin as long as buyers and sellers stick to differing price ideas, traders holding informal marketing discussions here said on Thursday.
"High prices were paid to farmers during a much delayed harvest and this means too much expensive grain is stuck somewhere in the marketing chain without moving," one said.

"Local consumers will sit this out and aim for price falls once the full weight of European supplies hits the market, but I fear for our export chances," the trader with an international grain house said.
Farmers were spoilt by high price prospects throughout the harvest due to tight global grain markets and because empty stocks meant storeholders initially paid high prices.
Wheat farmgate prices for example were 20-40 marks above those last year during the harvest and are still 15 marks up in a 250-270 mark range in the export-intensive North.

German prices held firm levels in recent weeks although bumper crops in Europe and worldwide were reported because eastern Europeans, namely Poland and Uzbekistan, needed German wheat to boost domestic supply.

"But this business is on hold at the moment and if it doesn't continue, there will be considerable downward pressure on prices amid competition from France, Britain and Denmark in markets across the EU (European Union)," an export broker said.

Although most Europan currencies and the dollar had weakened versus the mark -- and weakened German sales chances -- eastern and southern European millers need a certain amount of high protein wheat from Germany for blending.
Apart from demand and currency factors, export flows are also ruled by decisions in Brussels on the level of rebates.

Policy makers need to find a compromise between the need to export EU surpluses prior to the arrival of cheaper world market competitors, and to appease the United States, which will retaliate against overly generous EU subsidies.
Traders said today's weekly wheat subsidy may be set below 10 Ecus per tonne after 6.90 last week to enable EU exporters to compete with low-cost producer Argentina.
Germans today applied for rebates at 6.50-12.85 Ecus.
Unsold grain may be headed for intervention when the buying season starts in November, with a 230.50-mark minimum price.
Fob Baltic wheat is still quoted in a 287-315 mark range.
Apart from grain, traders at the 400-strong meeting also discussed upcoming winter trade in feeds and oilseeds.

"Protein feeds are firmer after overnight soya gains in Chicago, with rapemeal barely changed," said Heinz Ahrens, the president of the Bremen association of grains and feeds importers and wholesalers, which is hosting the meeting.
Bremen is a centre of feed import companies and logistics firms supplying nearby livestock industry centres.
A meals broker said feed mixers who were not overly busy needed to buy raw materials for the winter months, but ample feedgrain supply slowed soymeal and rapemeal sales.
"Only soymeal markets have started to liven up," he said.
An oilseeds broker said sellers still resisted price pressure although crushers could not afford domestic rapeseed.
"Crushers are using soybeans instead and processors use alternative oils bought in the Rotterdam market," one said.
